newsitem.title: THAILAND: Laws sought to curb global money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Laws sought to curb global money laundering.

text.p: Thai and international agencies on Tuesday called for stricter laws to curb money laundering which they said threatened global economic stability.
The joint appeal was made during an Asia money laundering symposium hosted by the international Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and Thailand's Office of Narcotics Control Board (ONCB).

"We gather here for two important reasons -- to recognise the threat that money laundering poses to economic stability of our countries and to establish effective mechanism to counter this phenomenon," FATF president Fernando Carpentienri told 170 delegates from 39 countries.
"Countries cannot afford to be without money laundering legislation if they want to attract long-term legitimate business. Therefore effective countermeasures are required...," he said.
The FATF cannot take action against money laundering but can make recommendations to governments to help curb it.
Thailand, a main conduit for drugs from the Golden Triangle and a centre of prostitution, has expressed hopes that its own draft anti-money laundering laws will help curb transfers of illicit funds.

"You see Thailand is a haven for criminals to launder black money but I am confident when the new law comes into effect, we can curb and deter their activities," said Thai legal expert Chaiyod Hemarachatha, who chaired a sub-committee drafting the anti-money laundering law.

He quoted a research report by economists at Bangkok's Chulalongkorn University as saying that Thailand attracted up to 800 billion baht ($30.8 billion) in illegal money each year from narcotics, prostitution, gambling and smuggling.
"Thailand is the main drugs route originated in the Golden Triangle and a massive amount of black money is laundered here," Chaiyod said.
He said financial institutions, especially banks, were the main route. "Banks, hotels, restaurants and many service sectors are part of money laundering networks used by drugs syndicates."
ONCB chief Preecha Champarat said the Thai anti-laundering law was being scrutinised by parliament.
